Zheng He's voyages were seven expeditions of the Ming treasure fleet, sent between 1405 and 1433 across the South China Sea and the Indian Ocean, as far as Arabia and East Africa. They were led by Zheng He, a Muslim court eunuch from Yunnan.

The Yongle Emperor ordered the fleet in 1403. Six voyages sailed in his reign and a seventh under the Xuande Emperor. The aims were to show Ming power, draw foreign rulers into sending tribute, and control trade. The fleets were huge, with tens of thousands of men and large treasure ships whose real size is still argued over.

  • The first three voyages went as far as Calicut in India.
  • The fourth reached Hormuz in the Persian Gulf.
  • The last three went on to Arabia and the East African coast, to Mogadishu and Malindi among the Swahili towns.

The fleets fought pirates near Palembang and a king in Sri Lanka. Envoys came back with them, and giraffes from Africa were presented at court, where they were taken for the mythical qilin.

After Yongle died in 1424, officials argued the voyages cost too much, and after 1433 they stopped. The Ming turned to defending the northern frontier and limited private sea trade. Sixty-five years later the Portuguese arrived in the same waters when Vasco da Gama reached Calicut, at the far end of the Indian Ocean trade network.
